Eigenvalues and singular values

Source: vignettes/spectral.Rmd
spectral.Rmd

Installation 

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/linop")

Installing linop installs one package. There are no Imports and no compiled code, so there is no toolchain to have working first. Matrix sits in Suggests and is used for sparse leaves and as_sparse().

R 4.4.0 or newer. The floor is set by crossprod() and tcrossprod(), which became S3 generic in R 4.4.0, and are what let one matrixOps method cover all three matrix products.

Two verbs

eigs() computes a few eigenpairs of a square operator. svds() computes a few singular triplets of any operator. Both run against the action alone, and both hold ncv vectors rather than a matrix.

The 1D Laplacian has closed-form eigenvalues, which makes it the fixture to check against:

n <- 200
lap <- function(X) 2 * X - rbind(X[-1, , drop = FALSE], 0) - rbind(0, X[-n, , drop = FALSE])
L <- linop(lap, adjoint = lap, dim = c(n, n), properties = c(hermitian = TRUE))

truth <- 2 - 2 * cos(seq_len(n) * pi / (n + 1))

fit <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", method = "lanczos", ncv = 60)
fit
#> <lanczos> 3 of 3 requested eigenpairs converged, which = 'largest_algebraic'
#>   450 iterations of at most 4000, 12 restarts
#>   values: 3.999756  3.999023  3.997802
#>   certificate: qualified
rbind(computed = fit$values,
      closed_form = rev(sort(truth))[1:3])
#>                 [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
#> computed    3.999756 3.999023 3.997802
#> closed_form 3.999756 3.999023 3.997802

Hermitian or not

eigs() has two methods. Lanczos is defined for a hermitian operator, and its projected problem is a real symmetric tridiagonal matrix. Arnoldi with Krylov-Schur restarting runs on any square operator. Symmetry is not probed and not assumed, so a callback that declares nothing gets Arnoldi:

Undeclared <- linop(lap, adjoint = lap, dim = c(n, n))
plain <- eigs(Undeclared, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", ncv = 60)
plain$method
#> [1] "arnoldi"
plain$values - rev(sort(truth))[1:3]
#> [1] 8.881784e-16 1.332268e-15 4.440892e-16

The values are right, and the dispatch says why Lanczos was passed over:

d <- plain$certificate$dispatch$candidates
d[d$backend %in% c("lanczos", "arnoldi"), c("backend", "status")]
#>   backend   status
#> 2 lanczos rejected
#> 3 arnoldi selected
d$reason[d$backend == "lanczos"]
#> [1] "requires the operator to be hermitian; it declares hermitian = NA, and unknown is not false"

Unknown is not false, and the dispatch says so rather than guessing either way. A dense leaf establishes symmetry by checking it, so a matrix needs no declaration; a callback has nothing to check and the declaration is how you supply it.

A declaration is your word, and method = "auto" does not act on it alone. It takes Lanczos when symmetry is computed, constructed or proven, as solve() takes MINRES only then, and otherwise runs Arnoldi and says why. Naming the method is how you rely on your own declaration, which is why the calls on L in this article say method = "lanczos":

eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", ncv = 60)$method
#> [1] "arnoldi"
d <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", ncv = 60)$certificate$dispatch$candidates
d$reason[d$backend == "lanczos"]
#> [1] "auto acts on hermitian only at computed, constructed or proven evidence, and the operator's is user_declaration; name the method to rely on it"

Whichever method runs, the declaration buys a bound on the eigenvalues, the forward error row of the certificate, and that row records the declaration it rests on:

row <- function(fit, check) fit$certificate$checks$status[fit$certificate$checks$check == check]
c(declared = row(fit, "forward error"), undeclared = row(plain, "forward error"))
#>      declared    undeclared 
#>        "pass" "not_checked"

A non-normal operator

Convection-diffusion on a grid, 2 u_j - (1 + mu) u_{j-1} - (1 - mu) u_{j+1}, is not symmetric for mu != 0, and its eigenvalues are still known in closed form, 2 - 2 sqrt(1 - mu^2) cos(j pi / (n + 1)). Its eigenvectors are the sine vectors scaled by rho^j, rho = sqrt((1 + mu)/(1 - mu)), so they are far from orthogonal once rho^n is large.

convdiff <- function(n, mu) {
  force(n); force(mu)
  linop(function(X) 2 * X - (1 + mu) * rbind(0, X[-n, , drop = FALSE]) -
                    (1 - mu) * rbind(X[-1, , drop = FALSE], 0), dim = c(n, n))
}
cd_truth <- function(n, mu) 2 - 2 * sqrt(1 - mu^2) * cos(seq_len(n) * pi / (n + 1))

mild <- eigs(convdiff(80, 0.04), k = 3, which = "largest_real")
mild$values - sort(cd_truth(80, 0.04), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
#> [1] -7.993606e-15  3.552714e-14 -2.975398e-13

At mu = 0.04 and n = 80, rho^n is 24 and the values agree with the closed form to rounding. At mu = 0.5 and n = 100 it is 3^50, and the same computation goes differently:

hard <- eigs(convdiff(100, 0.5), k = 2, which = "largest_real")
hard$values - sort(cd_truth(100, 0.5), decreasing = TRUE)[1:2]
#> [1] 0.03611324+0.01361576i 0.03862589-0.01361577i
hard$certificate
#> solved by arnoldi (operator not established hermitian, Arnoldi with Krylov-Schur restarting (highest priority eligible; primme requires the operator to be hermitian; it declares hermitian = NA, and unknown is not false; lanczos requires the operator to be hermitian; it declares hermitian = NA, and unknown is not false))
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         computation      estimate              -
#> residual                       pass         computation      identity              1
#> orthogonality                  not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> backward error                 pass         computation      estimate              -
#> target identity                not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> convergence                    pass         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        qualified   no deterministic bound on: arithmetic floor, orthogonality, backward error, target identity, forward error

The backward error passes: each value is an exact eigenvalue of an operator within tol ||A|| of this one. The eigenvalues of this operator move by far more than that under such a perturbation, which is what an eigenvector condition number of 3^50 means, so the computed values are wrong in the first digit, and they come back as a complex pair although every eigenvalue is real. The certificate does not claim otherwise. Its forward error row places each value in the operator’s pseudospectrum and stops there, because the bound from there to an eigenvalue needs the eigenvector condition number, and that is not computed. The orthogonality row is not checked either, since these eigenvectors are not orthogonal.

A real operator’s non-real eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs, and eigs() computes the two members together, so asking for k values that end inside a pair still returns both members converged. which takes "largest_imaginary" and "smallest_imaginary" for the magnitude of the imaginary part, and a complex sigma for the values nearest a point off the real axis.

svds() works on any operator and is sometimes the thing that was actually wanted: singular values are well conditioned whatever the eigenvectors are.

ncv is the knob that matters

ncv is how many vectors a restart holds. Each restart compresses the subspace to the vectors it keeps, so the smaller ncv is, the more applies the method spends reaching the tolerance:

ladder <- t(vapply(c(20, 30, 40, 60), function(nc) {
  f <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", method = "lanczos", ncv = nc)
  c(ncv = nc,
    error = max(abs(f$values - rev(sort(truth))[1:3])),
    converged = f$nconv,
    applies = f$iterations)
}, numeric(4)))
ladder
#>      ncv        error converged applies
#> [1,]  20 8.881784e-16         3     618
#> [2,]  30 4.440892e-16         3     493
#> [3,]  40 4.440892e-16         3     460
#> [4,]  60 8.881784e-16         3     450

The top of the Laplacian’s spectrum is tightly clustered, which is what makes a small subspace slow here. A well-separated spectrum needs far fewer applies.

The budget maxit counts applies, and its default is 20 n: twenty times what forming the operator column by column would cost. It grows with n because a crowded end of the spectrum gets more crowded as n grows, and at a fixed ncv the applies grow with it: the reference Lanczos takes 1.6 n for the three largest here and 6 n at n = 2000. At the defaults the run converges well inside it:

dflt <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", method = "lanczos")
c(converged = dflt$nconv, applies = dflt$iterations, budget = dflt$maxit)
#> converged   applies    budget 
#>         3       549      4000

A run that stops improving ends before the budget does and says so, so a larger default costs time only on a run that is still converging. The far end of a spectrum spread over many decades is the case it does not cover; a shift near that end, sigma, is the tool there.

What gets reported is the Rayleigh quotient

The value attached to each vector is x^H A x / (x^H x), measured against A itself rather than read off the projected problem. It is the choice of mu that minimises ||A x - mu x||, so no other value certifies better for the vector that was found.

That matters most under a shift, where the projected problem is a solve against A - sigma I and its own accuracy is a separate question. Measuring on A means nothing downstream inherits the inner solve’s error.

Which end 

c(largest  = eigs(L, k = 2, which = "largest_algebraic", method = "lanczos", ncv = 60)$values,
  smallest = eigs(L, k = 2, which = "smallest_algebraic", method = "lanczos", ncv = 40)$values)
#>     largest1     largest2    smallest1    smallest2 
#> 3.9997557139 3.9990229152 0.0002442861 0.0009770848

"largest" and "smallest" order by magnitude, "largest_algebraic" and "smallest_algebraic" by value. For an operator with a negative eigenvalue those are different questions. RSpectra’s "LM", "SM", "LA" and "SA" are accepted for the same four, so existing calling code ports without edits.

Eigenvalues near a point

sigma runs the same recurrence on (A - sigma I)^-1, and that inverse is not formed: it is the package’s own solvers, applied once per step.

near <- eigs(L, k = 3, sigma = 0.01, method = "lanczos", ncv = 30,
             inner = list(method = "minres"))
rbind(computed = sort(near$values),
      closed_form = sort(truth[order(abs(truth - 0.01))][1:3]))
#>                   [,1]        [,2]       [,3]
#> computed    0.00610417 0.008788036 0.01195833
#> closed_form 0.00610417 0.008788036 0.01195833

inner carries the arguments for that solve, so its method and tolerance are yours to set. This is the one place the two halves of the package meet: everything in vignette("solvers") is available inside a spectral computation.

A shift costs a full linear solve per expansion step.

Harmonic extraction

target selects eigenvalues near a point using a Krylov space built by applying A. With extraction = "harmonic", the projection uses the reciprocals of Ritz values of the shifted inverse on (A - target I) V. The computation uses a small projected problem. Lanczos and Arnoldi both retain the wanted harmonic Schur space and its residual direction at each restart.

harmonic <- eigs(L, k = 3, target = 2.02, extraction = "harmonic",
                 method = "lanczos", ncv = 40)
cbind(computed = harmonic$values,
      closed_form = truth[order(abs(truth - 2.02))][1:3])
#>      computed closed_form
#> [1,] 2.015630    2.015630
#> [2,] 2.046885    2.046885
#> [3,] 1.984370    1.984370
row(harmonic, "backward error")
#> [1] "pass"

target applies A directly at every step; sigma invokes shift-invert. They are mutually exclusive. The finite standard problem supports harmonic extraction, with a real target for a real or hermitian operator. Ordinary Rayleigh-Ritz extraction is available with target through extraction = "ritz". Interior convergence depends on the subspace size and the spectrum. Harmonic extraction may take more expansion steps than shift-invert, whose steps each include a solve.

Each returned value is the Rayleigh quotient of the harmonic Ritz vector, measured on A. The eigenpair certificate and its stopping rule apply directly.

A second operator on the right

A finite-element discretisation puts a mass matrix on the right-hand side, K u = lambda M u. For linear elements on the unit interval the stiffness is the Laplacian above and the mass is tridiag(1, 4, 1) / 6; the two share the sine eigenvectors, so the pencil’s eigenvalues are known in closed form, 6 (1 - cos t) / (2 + cos t) with t = j pi / (n + 1):

mass <- function(X) (4 * X + rbind(X[-1, , drop = FALSE], 0) +
                     rbind(0, X[-n, , drop = FALSE])) / 6
M <- linop(mass, adjoint = mass, dim = c(n, n),
           properties = c(hermitian = TRUE, positive_definite = TRUE))
t_j <- seq_len(n) * pi / (n + 1)
pencil_truth <- sort(6 * (1 - cos(t_j)) / (2 + cos(t_j)), decreasing = TRUE)

gen <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", method = "lanczos", B = M, ncv = 60)
gen$values - pencil_truth[1:3]
#> [1]  1.776357e-15 -3.552714e-15  0.000000e+00

B is the argument. With A hermitian and B hermitian positive definite, Lanczos runs on B^-1 A in the inner product x^H B x, where that operator is self-adjoint, so the projected problem stays real and symmetric. Each step solves with B, by the package’s own solvers, and inner carries that solve’s arguments as it does under a shift. The vectors come back orthonormal in the same inner product:

max(abs(crossprod(gen$vectors, mass(gen$vectors)) - diag(3)))
#> [1] 1.110223e-15

Without the two declarations on B the same call runs Arnoldi on B^-1 A and says why in the dispatch. The certificate measures each pair as x^H A x / x^H B x and perturbs both operators in its backward error, ||A x - theta B x|| / ((||A|| + |theta| ||B||) ||x||), since a pencil’s data is the pair. sigma with B runs on (A - sigma B)^-1 B.

Singular values

svds() needs both the forward action and the adjoint, and requires nothing else:

G <- matrix(rnorm(60 * 12), 60, 12)
R <- linop(G)

sv <- svds(R, k = 2)
rbind(computed = sv$d, closed_form = svd(G)$d[1:2])
#>                 [,1]     [,2]
#> computed    11.17144 10.08422
#> closed_form 11.17144 10.08422

The triplets satisfy what they should:

c(`A v - d u` = max(abs(G %*% sv$v - sv$u %*% diag(sv$d))),
  `U orthonormal` = max(abs(crossprod(sv$u) - diag(2))),
  `V orthonormal` = max(abs(crossprod(sv$v) - diag(2))))
#>     A v - d u U orthonormal V orthonormal 
#>  8.881784e-16  2.220446e-16  2.220446e-16

Underneath, this is eigs() on the hermitian augmented operator

H = [ 0    A  ]
    [ A^H  0  ]

whose eigenpairs are (sigma, [u; v]/sqrt(2)). H is hermitian for every A with nothing to declare, which is why svds() asks the operator for no properties where eigs() asks for one. One consequence is worth knowing: the certificate’s orthogonality row measures the augmented basis, where a deviation in U could cancel one in V, so the check above measures the two separately.

which = "smallest" is accepted and is the hard end of the problem. A Krylov space reaches the largest singular values first, so the smallest need a subspace approaching the rank of the operator:

small <- svds(R, k = 2, which = "smallest", ncv = 12)
rbind(computed = small$d, closed_form = rev(svd(G)$d)[1:2])
#>                 [,1]     [,2]
#> computed    4.746325 5.603087
#> closed_form 4.746325 5.603087

The request is not refused. What was reached is reported, and the certificate is where you find out whether it was enough.

A result that is right and certifies as qualified

This is worth meeting once, because it looks like a hedge and is not:

smallest <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "smallest_algebraic", method = "lanczos", ncv = 40)

rbind(computed = smallest$values, closed_form = sort(truth)[1:3])
#>                     [,1]         [,2]        [,3]
#> computed    0.0002442861 0.0009770848 0.002198217
#> closed_form 0.0002442861 0.0009770848 0.002198217
smallest$certificate$overall
#> [1] "qualified"

Every value is right to the last printed digit and the certificate says qualified. The reason is in which row is qualified:

smallest$certificate
#> solved by lanczos (hermitian operator, Lanczos with full reorthogonalisation (requested by name))
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         computation      estimate              -
#> residual                       pass         computation      identity              1
#> orthogonality                  pass         computation      identity              1
#> backward error                 pass         computation      estimate              -
#> target identity                not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> convergence                    pass         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  pass         theorem          deterministic_bound   1
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        qualified   no deterministic bound on: arithmetic floor, backward error, target identity

backward error and forward error, which is a rigorous bound here, pass with room to spare. The row that does not is residual, which divides by |theta|, and the smallest eigenvalue of this operator is 2.4e-4. A residual near the arithmetic floor is still large relative to a tiny eigenvalue, so the pair meets the tolerance only once the floor is added to it, and qualified is the status that says so.

overall is a summary of seven rows, and each row answers its own question. The rows are what to read. vignette("certificates") covers what each one measures.
